displayQuote: Venice Streets Are Full of Water. Please Advise

meta.title: Who really said "Venice Streets Are Full of Water. Please Advise"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Robert Benchley sent it; David Niven received it. And the cable did not say “please” — the earliest text reads “Streets full of water. Advise.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Venice Streets Are Full of Water. Please Advise'?
meta.ogDescription: Benchley wrote the cable, Niven got it and told the story. The famous wording is a later tidy-up. Sources and dates.

answer.label: Not David Niven — actually Robert Benchley
answer.authorDates: 15 September 1889 – 21 November 1945 · American humorist and “New Yorker” writer
answer.sourceLine: Benchley sent the cable; David Niven received it. Niven had arranged the trip and later told the story in print, which is how his name drifted onto the joke. The wording drifted too: the earliest published text is “STREETS FULL OF WATER. ADVISE” — no “Venice,” no “please.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Bulletin from Benchley,” “The Reader’s Digest,” October 1958, p. 52 — credited “As told to Dean Jennings in The Saturday Evening Post”
Not recorded. Quote Investigator judges it “probably in the late 1930s”

source.excerpt: David Niven tells about the time he and Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., planned a European itinerary for humorist Robert Benchley: “I made arrangements for him to visit some friends of mine in Venice. The day Benchley got there he sent us a cable which read: STREETS FULL OF WATER. ADVISE.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ was prompted by exactly the problem this page exists to solve: a reader found a 1958 newspaper version credited to a traveller named Mattie Barwick and wondered whether Benchley — who died in 1945 — was being given credit for something he never sent.

QI’s answer is that he did send it. The earliest text it locates is in “The Reader’s Digest” of October 1958, reprinting a “Saturday Evening Post” piece in which Niven himself tells the story — which both predates the Barwick version and identifies Benchley as the sender and Niven as the recipient.

Niven told it again in his 1972 memoir “The Moon’s a Balloon,” where QI transcribes the cable ↗ as “STREETS FULL OF WATER. ADVISE” above Benchley’s name; QI notes the book gives no date for it. The Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for the memoir ↗, though its scanned copy is a later printing and is lending-restricted.

The “please” is traceable drift: QI shows it first appearing in a 1962 Schenectady newspaper ↗, which also changed the recipient from a friend to a magazine. QI further transcribes ↗ the 1968 anthology “The Algonquin Wits” — the source the Yale Book of Quotations relies on — shortening it to “STREETS FLOODED. PLEASE ADVISE.” The Internet Archive has a catalogue record for that anthology ↗.
source.excerptNote: From “Bulletin from Benchley” in “The Reader’s Digest” of October 1958, as transcribed by Quote Investigator. This is the earliest text of the cable we could trace — and it contains neither the word “Venice” nor the word “please.”

source.rightsNote: The cable was probably sent in the late 1930s, but it first reached print in 1958 — in a “Saturday Evening Post” article by Dean Jennings, reprinted in “The Reader’s Digest” that October — and again in Niven’s “The Moon’s a Balloon” in 1972. Both are well after the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff, so the text as published is in copyright.

author.name: Robert Benchley
author.heading: About Robert Benchley
author.bio: Robert Benchley was a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table and for years the drama critic of The New Yorker, where he perfected a style of comic essay built on the bewilderment of a reasonable man in an unreasonable world. He later moved to Hollywood, won an Academy Award for the 1935 short How to Sleep, and appeared in dozens of films. The Venice cable is entirely characteristic: the joke is that he is the only person behaving sensibly.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Almost everything about this quotation travels badly: the author, the wording, and the person it was sent to. Only the joke survives intact.

items.why: Niven arranged Benchley’s trip, received the cable, and told the story in print twice — in a 1958 “Saturday Evening Post” piece ↗ and in his 1972 memoir. Telling a joke well for fifty years is how a recipient becomes an author.

The earliest text has no “please”: it is “STREETS FULL OF WATER. ADVISE.” QI dates the “please” to a 1962 newspaper retelling ↗, and QI’s own conclusion is that “the most common modern versions are stated differently than the original text.”
A 2005 “San Francisco Chronicle” version has Benchley wiring the magazine, as QI records ↗. The earliest account has him wiring Niven, a friend who had booked the trip.

A Miami News column of 30 October 1958 gave the line to a traveller of that name, which is what set QI’s investigation going ↗. It appeared weeks after the Benchley version was already in national circulation.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: “there is evidence that Robert Benchley did send a witty telegram about Venice to the prominent actor David Niven probably in the late 1930s… The most common modern versions are stated differently than the original text.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a tiny masterpiece of form. A telegram charged by the word, a city everyone knows is built on canals, and a man reporting the obvious back to the person who sent him there — it is a whole comic situation in six words, which is why it has outlived almost everything else Benchley wrote.

It is also a good demonstration of why wording matters. “Streets full of water. Advise.” is funnier than the tidied-up version, because “advise” alone is the clipped idiom of a real cable. Adding “please” makes it polite, and politeness is not the joke.
detailsBody: The reader who wrote to Quote Investigator had spotted something genuinely suspicious: a 1958 newspaper gave the line to an ordinary tourist, Benchley had been dead thirteen years, and the earliest reference books crediting him only appeared in 1968. On that evidence the Benchley attribution looks like a famous name absorbing an anonymous joke.

What rescued it was finding the 1958 Reader’s Digest item, in which Niven tells the story himself and names Benchley. That reversed the chronology — the Benchley version was in national circulation before the tourist version, not after it. The attribution survived; the exact wording did not.
context.pull: Adding “please” makes it polite, and politeness is not the joke.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator locates the earliest text of the cable in The Reader’s Digest of October 1958 as “STREETS FULL OF WATER. ADVISE”, in an item where David Niven names Benchley as the sender and himself as the recipient.

Quote Investigator concludes Benchley did send the telegram to Niven probably in the late 1930s, and that modern versions are worded differently from the original; it dates the added “please” to a 1962 Schenectady newspaper.
Robert Benchley lived 15 September 1889 to 21 November 1945 and was an American humorist.
David Niven lived 1910 to 1983 and was a British actor.
